strengths: Provides a mathematically rigorous, closed-form derivation for ray-Gaussian transmittance that removes the linear/projective (EWA/UT) approximation error inherent to splatting-based 3DGS variants, with a clean canonical-coordinate proof (Theorem 1) and full gradient derivations in the appendix.

Introduces Particle Bounding Frustum (PBF) association, an efficient closed-form (quadratic-equation) alternative to BVH traversal or Unscented-Transform-based conic approximation; empirically shown to yield 2.5-5x fewer Gaussians per tile and clear runtime gains over EWA/UT association (Tab. K.5, K.6).

Proposes the Bipolar Equiangular Projection (BEAP), a camera-agnostic image parameterization that unifies pinhole/fisheye supervision and yields more uniform angular ray sampling, with a dedicated ablation (Sec. 4.5, Table 6) showing consistent gains over perspective/equidistant supervision.

Extensive empirical validation spanning four datasets (ScanNet++, ZipNeRF, Aria, MipNeRF360) with both fisheye and pinhole cameras, including cross-camera generalization (fisheye-to-pinhole and vice versa), extreme/out-of-distribution FoV generalization, and central-vs-peripheral region analysis -- all supporting the central claim of reduced approximation error under wide FoV.

Careful ablations isolate the contribution of each component: transmittance formulation vs. splatting approximation (Sec 4.4, Fig 8), association strategy (Table K.6), and BEAP supervision (Table 6), plus a Gaussian-count scaling study (Fig. 5) directly rebutting a concurrent claim (Celarek et al. 2025) that brute-force scaling closes the approximation gap.

Thorough appendix with full derivations, numerical-stability discussion (including a concrete demonstration of a competing method's instability, Fig. C.1), algorithmic pseudocode, and a discussion contextualizing the method relative to 2DGS/HTGS and prior ray-tracing methods (3DGRT/3DGUT/EVER).

Runtime comparable to or approaching optimized 3DGS splatting (Table 4, Table K.4) while retaining exactness, and about 5x faster than prior projective-exact ray-based baselines, which is a meaningful systems contribution beyond the geometric derivation.
weaknesses: The title/abstract claim of rendering being made fully 'exact' is somewhat overstated; Appendix A explicitly admits the method still relies on maximum-response/ordering approximations and does not resolve self-occlusion or overlapping attenuation exactly, which should be more prominently flagged in the main text rather than relegated to a limitations appendix.

The mirror-transformation trick (Sec D.2, with heuristic parameter ξ=1 fixed across all experiments) used to handle PBF-CSF intersection outside the monotonic tan domain is somewhat ad hoc; sensitivity of results to this hyperparameter, and behavior at or near 180° circular FoV boundaries, is not analyzed.

The method introduces substantial additional complexity (canonical transforms, PBF quadratic solves, mirror angle bookkeeping, BEAP inverse interpolation) relative to 3DGS; although runtime is competitive, the implementation/engineering burden and reproducibility risk are nontrivially higher, and code is only promised, not yet available for review.

Evaluation is centered on indoor/bounded or moderate-scale scenes (ScanNet++, Aria, MipNeRF360 objects); there is limited evidence of behavior on very large-scale outdoor/unbounded scenes or highly dynamic content, where ordering/self-occlusion approximations (acknowledged as a limitation) may matter more.

The paper reports an extremely large number of tables/ablations (K.1-K.9) which, while thorough, makes it hard to discern which comparisons are most central; some presentation streamlining between main text and appendix could improve clarity.

All baselines appear to be self-reimplemented/reproduced by the authors (with some numbers sourced from original papers only for the FPS metric), so there is some risk of reproduction bias favoring the proposed method, though this is common practice in the field.

strengths: Provides a rigorous, first-principles derivation of a closed-form, projective-exact transmittance integral for ray-based 3D Gaussian rendering via a canonical isotropic transformation, with a full gradient cookbook and numerical-stability analysis (Appendix B-C).

Proposes Particle Bounding Frustum (PBF) association that replaces costly BVH traversal or sampling-based Unscented Transform with a closed-form frustum-ellipsoid intersection, yielding a measured 2.5-5x speedup in the association stage and tile-association counts ~3-5x tighter than EWA/UT (Tab. K.5-K.6), while retaining geometric exactness that EWA/UT lack.

Introduces Bipolar Equiangular Projection (BEAP), a camera-agnostic image parameterization that unifies pinhole/fisheye FoVs, improves ray sampling uniformity, and is shown via controlled ablation (Table 6, Fig. K.5) to outperform perspective/equidistant supervision spaces.

Extensive empirical validation across four diverse datasets (ScanNet++, ZipNeRF with cross-camera generalization, MipNeRF360, Aria egocentric), with consistent PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS gains over strong and recent baselines (3DGS, FisheyeGS, EVER, 3DGUT, 3DGRT), plus a careful scaling study (Fig. 5) showing that naive Gaussian-count scaling cannot close the approximation gap that 3DGEER closes by construction.

Thorough and honest ablations isolate each component's contribution (transmittance formulation vs. association scheme vs. BEAP supervision), and the appendix explicitly discusses limitations (no explicit self-occlusion/ordering resolution) rather than overselling exactness.

Runtime analysis demonstrates the method achieves speeds comparable to splatting-based 3DGS (327 vs 343 FPS) while being >5x faster than other projective-exact ray-based methods (3DGRT, EVER), addressing a genuine efficiency-accuracy trade-off gap in the literature.
weaknesses: The core 'maximum-response' ray-Gaussian interaction model is inherited from prior work (Keselman & Hebert, 2022; 3DGRT/3DGUT) rather than newly proposed; the paper's exactness claim pertains specifically to association/rendering geometry and explicitly does not resolve self-occlusion, ordering, or overlap effects (acknowledged in Appendix A), which somewhat tempers the 'geometrically exact' framing used throughout the main text and title.

Quantitative gains on standard narrow-FoV pinhole benchmarks (e.g., MipNeRF360, Table 4: 27.76 vs 3DGS 27.21 and EVER 27.51 PSNR) are modest, suggesting the main practical benefit is concentrated in wide-FoV/fisheye settings rather than being a universal improvement.

Several auxiliary design choices (e.g., the mirror parameter ξ=1 used 'throughout all experiments' in the CMEI-inspired angular correction, Appendix D.2) are fixed heuristically without sensitivity analysis or justification, raising reproducibility/robustness questions for cameras with very different distortion profiles.

The method introduces considerable additional complexity (canonical transformation, closed-form quadratic PBF solver, mirror-angle correction for extreme FoV, BEAP projection/inverse interpolation) relative to baselines, which may hinder adoption and independent verification; code is not yet released (promised only post-publication), limiting immediate reproducibility despite the detailed math appendix.

Popping artifacts from unresolved depth ordering/self-attenuation are acknowledged but not quantitatively characterized (e.g., no frequency/severity metric across scenes), leaving an important practical limitation under-evaluated.

Dataset/evaluation protocols (e.g., custom central/peripheral region splits on ScanNet++, cross-camera ZipNeRF alignment using SfM poses from only one camera type) are bespoke to this paper, which could complicate fair comparison with future work and raises minor concerns about protocol-induced advantages.

strengths: Provides a genuinely novel closed-form derivation for ray-Gaussian transmittance via a canonical isotropic coordinate transform, cleanly connecting the heuristic 'maximum response' assumption used in prior ray-tracing work to a rigorous projective-exact formulation.

Introduces the Particle Bounding Frustum (PBF) association scheme that replaces costly BVH traversal with closed-form frustum-particle intersection tests, achieving 2.5-5x speedups in association while avoiding the projective approximation errors (and resulting grid-line/mismatched culling artifacts) of EWA/UT-based methods.

The Bipolar Equiangular Projection (BEAP) is a simple but effective idea for balanced ray sampling under wide-FoV cameras, and the ablation (Table 6) convincingly shows it outperforms perspective/equidistant alternatives.

Extensive and diverse experimental validation across fisheye (ScanNet++, ZipNeRF, Aria) and pinhole (MipNeRF360, ZipNeRF) datasets, including cross-camera generalization (train pinhole/test fisheye and vice versa) and extreme-FoV generalization studies, which is uncommon in this literature.

Thoughtful and thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each component: exact transmittance vs. splatting approximation, PBF vs. EWA/UT association, BEAP vs. alternative supervision spaces, and a careful comparison against naive Gaussian-count scaling as an alternative to exactness (Celarek et al.).

Detailed appendix with full mathematical derivations (transmittance integral proof, backward gradient cookbook, PBF solver, mirror-angle correction for wide-FoV association) and numerical stability discussion, which supports reproducibility and rigor.

Runtime is competitive with 3DGS/splatting-based approaches while being ~5x faster than exact ray-marching/tracing baselines (3DGRT, EVER), demonstrating that exactness and efficiency are not mutually exclusive as claimed.

Honest limitations section (Appendix A) acknowledging that ordering/self-occlusion is still handled via depth sorting rather than being fully exact, which is refreshing compared to the possibly overclaiming abstract.
weaknesses: The term 'exact' is used quite liberally in the title/abstract, yet the method still relies on depth-sorted alpha compositing rather than truly resolving self-occlusion/ordering (as EVER does, at a speed cost); this nuance is only clarified deep in Appendix A and could mislead readers if they only see the abstract/title.

Gains on standard narrow-FoV pinhole benchmarks (e.g., MipNeRF360, Table 4: 27.76 vs 3DGS 27.21 PSNR) are quite modest, suggesting the core benefit is concentrated in wide-FoV/fisheye regimes; the paper's framing as a general-purpose 'made exact and efficient for generic cameras' method is only strongly justified in the distorted-camera setting.

The overall pipeline (CSF/PBF/BEAP/mirror-transform angular bounds) is mathematically intricate with several hand-set hyperparameters (e.g., mirror parameter ξ=1, λ=3 for ellipsoid bound) that are not ablated, raising questions about sensitivity and generality across camera models/scenes.

Evaluation is limited to room-scale/object-scale indoor or bounded outdoor scenes (ScanNet++, ZipNeRF, Aria, MipNeRF360); despite motivating the work with autonomous driving/robotics applications, no large-scale outdoor or driving datasets are tested, leaving scalability to large scenes with many more Gaussians unverified.

Some baselines (3DGUT, 3DGRT) are only lightly discussed qualitatively for failure cases (Appendix I) rather than being fully quantitatively stress-tested under the same extreme-FoV/generalization protocols applied to the proposed method.

The paper is very dense/appendix-heavy (35 pages), and reproducibility, while aided by promised code release, is difficult to fully verify from the manuscript alone given the many interacting closed-form solvers.
